past_medical_history: Prior ischemic stroke — right MCA territory, 3 years ago (residual left arm weakness, NIHSS 2 at baseline)

social_history.recent_stressor: Son involved in serious motor vehicle accident (hospitalized in ICU) 10 days ago; patient unable to visit son due to own hospitalization

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Extremely worried about his son. Appears distracted.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal right side. Mild residual left facial droop (BASELINE from prior stroke).
neurological_exam.motor: Baseline: left arm 4/5 (prior stroke residual). NEW: LEFT LEG NOW 2/5 (was 5/5 at last neurology visit 4 months ago). Right side: 5/5. The NEW finding is critical — prior stroke was right MCA, which would cause left arm/face weakness but typically NOT isolated left leg weakness (leg is ACA territory). POSITIVE Hoover: left leg 5/5 during right leg contralateral flexion. Left leg strength 4/5 when examining prior arm weakness distraction.
neurological_exam.sensory: Left leg sensory loss — does not follow the prior stroke sensory distribution (prior stroke: left arm and face sensory involvement, not leg).
neurological_exam.reflexes: Baseline increased left upper extremity reflexes (from prior stroke). LEFT LEG REFLEXES: paradoxically decreased (would expect increased from cortical lesion). No new Babinski (left Babinski absent — expected increase in prior stroke but absent on left leg side).
neurological_exam.coordination: Normal right. Left arm: baseline deficit. Left leg: cannot test.
neurological_exam.gait: Left leg dragging — significantly worse than what would be expected from prior right MCA stroke.
neurological_exam.additional: DIAGNOSTIC PUZZLE: Patient has known prior right MCA stroke with residual left arm weakness. New left LEG weakness appears to be a new stroke. HOWEVER: right MCA territory does NOT supply the leg (that's ACA). Left leg should not be newly affected by right MCA territory worsening. This is the KEY to solving this puzzle — anatomical incongruence.

patient.chief_complaint: Acute worsening of left-sided weakness — 'much worse than baseline'
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. T is a 56-year-old retired factory worker with a history of right MCA ischemic stroke 3 years ago (residual left arm weakness, baseline NIHSS 2) who presents with acute worsening of left-sided weakness over 4 days. At baseline, he has mild left arm weakness from his prior stroke. He now reports his left leg is newly and severely weak, and feels the left arm is also slightly worse. His son was involved in a serious motor vehicle accident 10 days ago and is currently in the ICU at a different hospital; the patient has been unable to visit and is extremely distressed. His blood pressure has been elevated (home readings 155-165/90-95). His diabetes has been poorly controlled (home glucose 200-280 mg/dL on self-monitoring). The immediate clinical concern is recurrent ischemic stroke. However, the anatomical puzzle is: his prior stroke was in the right MCA territory, which would not explain new LEFT LEG weakness. Left leg motor function is primarily controlled by the right ACA territory (medial motor cortex). New isolated left leg weakness suggesting ACA territory involvement is anatomically separate from his prior MCA stroke. Unless he has two simultaneous strokes (very unlikely) or a new ACA lesion, the left leg weakness requires another explanation.

findings.finding: Hoover sign LEFT LEG: When examiner applies resistance to right leg flexion, left leg hip extension returns to 5/5 (POSITIVE Hoover) — the baseline right MCA stroke involvement should leave left arm weak but NOT produce this pattern of left leg Hoover
Hoover sign LEFT ARM: When examiner applies resistance to right arm extension, left arm DOES NOT improve (remains 4/5 — this is the ORGANIC baseline stroke deficit)

Critical anatomical incongruence: Positive Hoover LEFT LEG but ABSENT Hoover LEFT ARM — this dissociation confirms the new left leg weakness is functional, while the chronic left arm weakness is organic (stroke)
Strength improvement left leg: 2/5 on direct testing → 4/5 when distracted during discussion of son's condition

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Functional neurological disorder — new functional left leg weakness superimposed on chronic organic left arm weakness from prior right MCA stroke (mixed organic + functional)

differential.key_features: Sudden focal deficit raises stroke; non-anatomical weakness pattern with positive Hoover sign, normal MRI/DWI, and intact reflexes argue against vascular etiology.
Focal complaints warrant imaging; normal brain MRI without lesion, mass, or enhancement effectively excludes a structural cause for the presenting deficit.
Non-dermatomal sensory loss, normal reflexes, and (when obtained) normal EMG/NCS argue against peripheral nerve or root pathology.
Episodic neurological symptoms can occur in autoimmune encephalitis; normal MRI, normal EEG background, and (when obtained) negative antibody panel render this very unlikely.

FND is involuntary; preserved effort on symptom-validity testing and absence of clear secondary gain argue against feigning. The rule-in signs do not distinguish FND from malingering by themselves, but the clinical context does not support a feigning explanation.

optimal_actions.action: Elicit positive rule-in signs on bedside examination (Hoover sign for functional leg weakness, tremor entrainment / distractibility for functional tremor, give-way weakness, non-dermatomal sensory loss with midline splitting). Diagnosis of FND is made by these positive signs, not by exclusion alone.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: At least one reliable positive functional sign documented

optimal_actions.action: Order brain MRI with and without contrast to exclude a structural cause of the presenting deficit
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No structural lesion, mass, demyelination, or stroke
optimal_actions.guideline_source: FND criteria pack — exclude structural cause

optimal_actions.action: Order basic laboratory workup (CBC, CMP, TSH, vitamin B12) to exclude common reversible mimics
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No metabolic, thyroid, or B12 abnormality that explains symptoms
optimal_actions.guideline_source: FND criteria pack — exclude reversible causes

optimal_actions.action: Search current literature on FND diagnostic signs and evidence-based treatment (CBT for PNES, specialized physiotherapy for functional motor symptoms)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Confirms multidisciplinary CBT + physiotherapy is the evidence-based treatment for FND

optimal_actions.action: Review current medications for agents that may exacerbate symptoms (e.g., benzodiazepines, dopamine-blocking antipsychotics, AEDs initiated for PNES)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Identification of medication contributors that should be tapered or discontinued

optimal_actions.action: Communicate the diagnosis transparently using positive language anchored on the rule-in signs; explicitly state the diagnosis is FND, the symptoms are real and involuntary, and there is an evidence-based treatment plan
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Patient understanding and treatment engagement — strong predictor of recovery

optimal_actions.action: Refer to specialized FND-informed physiotherapy (for functional motor symptoms) and to CBT / psychological therapy (for PNES and comorbid mood / anxiety)

useless_tools.rationale: ECG has no diagnostic role in FND; cardiac etiology is not on the differential for the presenting neurological deficit.
Echocardiography has no role in FND; no structural cardiac question is raised by the presentation.
Non-contrast head CT adds no information beyond MRI for an FND workup and contributes diagnostic noise plus radiation exposure.
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in typical FND; invasive testing reinforces somatic illness model and adds iatrogenic risk without changing management.
Advanced PET imaging has no indication in FND; standard MRI is the appropriate structural workup.

critical_actions: Document at least one positive rule-in sign (Hoover sign, tremor entrainment, distractibility, give-way pattern, non-dermatomal sensory loss with midline split)
Obtain brain MRI to exclude structural pathology
Communicate the diagnosis transparently using positive language and the rule-in signs as the basis
Refer for FND-informed physiotherapy and CBT / psychological therapy
Order a comprehensive neuropsychological battery to characterize comorbid depression, anxiety, somatization, and trauma exposure — informs treatment planning (criteria-pack 'recommended' tier)
contraindicated_actions: Do not pursue ever-expanding negative investigations — per Stone 2018, repeated negative workups reinforce illness conviction and worsen prognosis
Do not frame the diagnosis as 'all in your head', 'nothing wrong', or 'we couldn't find anything' — this damages the therapeutic alliance and is the most common avoidable harm in FND
Do not perform invasive testing (lumbar puncture, nerve biopsy, muscle biopsy, cerebral angiography) when positive rule-in signs are present and there is no clinical indication
Do not order EMG/NCS, muscle biopsy, or nerve biopsy as part of an FND workup — these invasive tests reinforce the somatic illness model per Stone 2018
key_reasoning_points: FND is a positive diagnosis based on rule-in signs (Hoover, tremor entrainment, give-way weakness, non-dermatomal sensory loss with midline split) — not a diagnosis of exclusion (Espay 2018, Stone 2018).
Brain MRI and basic labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12) are due-diligence to exclude structural and reversible causes — they are NOT the route to the diagnosis, which is established at the bedside.
Over-investigation is the principal iatrogenic harm in FND; every additional negative test reinforces the patient's illness conviction and worsens prognosis (Stone 2018).
Psychiatric comorbidity (anxiety, depression, trauma) is common and informs treatment planning but is NOT required for the diagnosis and does not 'explain' the symptoms in a reductive sense.
Diagnostic communication matters: using positive language anchored on the rule-in signs is associated with better engagement and outcomes (Stone 2018).
Evidence-based treatment is multidisciplinary — CBT for PNES and FND-informed physiotherapy for functional motor symptoms (Nielsen 2015).

red_herrings.data_point: Symptom onset coincident with a major psychosocial stressor
red_herrings.intended_effect: Conclude prematurely that stress 'caused' the symptoms and that the workup can be abbreviated
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Many organic conditions (MS, migraine, epilepsy) also flare with stress. Stress at onset is supportive context, not a diagnostic substitute for the positive rule-in signs.

metadata.notes: Diagnostic puzzle FND — functional left leg weakness in prior right MCA stroke patient. Anatomical incongruence is the key. Mixed organic+functional dissociation (Hoover positive leg, negative arm).
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Disabling, multi-region or refractory functional symptoms — often with comorbid organic disease (e.g., established MS, post-stroke deficit, prior epilepsy) or extensive prior workup. Differentiating new functional symptoms from organic progression requires careful synthesis of rule-in signs against negative imaging and EEG, plus discriminating communication.
